title: What Makes a Workplace Wellbeing Programme Actually Work?
excerpt: How sustainable wellbeing cultures are built, beyond one-off events.

body.text: Most organisations want their people to be well. The intention is genuine, and the budget is often real. Yet a great deal of what gets offered under the banner of wellbeing — the fruit basket, the one-off resilience webinar, the mindfulness app nobody remembers to open — quietly fails to make a difference. Not because the ideas are bad, but because wellbeing is being regarded as an event rather than a culture.

The question worth asking is not "what activity should we run?" but "what makes any of this actually stick?" Over years of working with teams, I have come to believe the answer has less to do with the programme itself and more to do with the conditions around it.
Why one-off events rarely change anything

A single wellbeing day can be genuinely good — a moment of pause, a useful idea, a sense of being cared for. But if people return to the same relentless workload, the same unspoken expectation to always be reachable, and the same manager who never switches off, the day evaporates within a week. Worse, it can breed quiet cynicism: the sense that wellbeing is something the organisation talks about rather than something it lives.
Sustainable wellbeing is not an intervention you apply to tired people. It is a set of everyday conditions that make it possible for people not to become depleted in the first place.
When wellbeing genuinely takes root in an organisation, a few things tend to be true underneath it. They are less glamorous than a headline event, but they are what makes the difference.

items: Leaders who model it — teams watch what leaders do far more than what they announce; a manager who protects their own boundaries gives everyone else permission to.
Workload that is honest — no amount of resilience training compensates for a job that is structurally impossible.
Psychological safety — people will only use support if they trust that admitting a struggle will not count against them.
Continuity — regular, familiar touchpoints rather than a single dramatic push.
A real say — wellbeing that is done with people, shaped by what they actually need, rather than delivered at them.

body.text: Notice how few of these are about a specific activity. The activity is the visible tip; the culture is what holds it up.

One of the most reliable shifts I see is when organisations stop thinking in campaigns and start thinking in rhythm. A short, regular touchpoint — something woven into the ordinary week — tends to do far more than an occasional grand gesture. It normalises looking after yourself, keeps wellbeing in view without making a fuss of it, and builds the small, repeated habits that a single event never can. This is the thinking behind the [weekly wellbeing sessions](/weekly-wellbeing) I run inside teams.

Rhythm also protects against the biggest enemy of workplace wellbeing: the always-on culture that equates constant availability with commitment. If your team never truly switches off, no programme will hold. It is worth reading more on [switching off from an always-on job](/blog/switching-off-always-on-job) as part of any serious wellbeing effort.
Meeting the group and the individual

Good workplace wellbeing works on two levels at once. There is the collective — the culture, the norms, the shared conditions — and there is the individual, because within any team some people will be quietly carrying more than others. A programme that only ever addresses the group can miss the person who most needs a confidential space, and one that only offers individual support can leave the culture that wore them down untouched.

In practice, this means combining group formats that shift the culture with the option of individual, confidential support for those who want it. You can see how I hold both together in [the work I do with organisations](/organisations).
Wellbeing is not something you bolt on to a stressful workplace. It is something you build into how the workplace works.

If your organisation has tried the one-off events and sensed that something deeper is needed, that instinct is worth trusting. The most effective programmes are rarely the flashiest — they are the ones patient enough to become part of the culture. That is slower work, but it is the work that lasts.
